paras: The attempted lynching of the Stubbs murder suspects took place at Polk City, Iowa, on the evening of 17 April 1882, when the town's vigilants stopped a train carrying men arrested for the killing of Mayor R. W. Stubbs. The vigilants took one prisoner off before prominent citizens persuaded them to let the prisoners go to the Des Moines county jail. Early wire reports that the suspects had been lynched were contradicted the same day.

Stubbs, mayor of Polk City and a partner in a milling firm, was shot dead in his house early on Saturday, 15 April, by intruders who fled on horses tied near the gate. After the firm's safe had been robbed, he kept its money at home because the town had no bank, and the intruders were thought to be after it. A Des Moines special to the Chicago Times reported that the town had a well-organized company of vigilantes who had acted in emergencies before and were out in force.

Five men were arrested, among them Job Weise, John Swin and Charles D. Errikson, whose names other papers spelled Wise, Swim and Derickson. According to a Des Moines dispatch of 17 April, vigilants guarded the prisoners until train time and then turned them over to officers, who put them aboard. As the train was ready to leave, the vigilants boarded it, opened a switch, placed an armed man at each brake and refused to let it start.

They took one prisoner off and tried to secure the others. Prominent citizens appealed to the leaders to let the law take its course, and the vigilants finally allowed the prisoners to be taken to Des Moines, where they were lodged in the county jail.

Wise, Swim and Derickson were arraigned at Polk City on the murder charge, and two other men, H. C. Saunders and Joe Cox, were arrested at Des Moines. In late June a young man named Delaire, arrested at the Polk City depot, confessed under threat of lynching that a gang of fifteen had plotted the robbery and that a man named Wicks fired the shot. Delaire was later released on a writ of habeas corpus and sued, saying he had been hanged until a false confession was forced from him. No report of a trial of any of the accused appears in the coverage.

The episode reached readers mainly through short telegraphic items in papers far from Iowa. The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer ran the first contradiction under the headline "Lynching Probable," saying that in the existing excitement a lynching was likely if the murderer could be identified. The Portland Daily Press headed its fuller account "Murderers Saved from Lynching," calling the prisoners murderers before any trial and closing that the danger of lynching had passed.

The Chicago Times special, reprinted in the Morris Tribune, dwelt on the mayor's character and wrote that if the vigilantes caught the murderers "the State will be spared the trouble of inflicting the penalty." None of the reports mentions the race of anyone involved, and no Black-press coverage of the episode was found.
